utterances.text: I would kindly ask you that we do not go into detail because I am really not familiar with the details. I don't want to be imprecise and therefore I would rather not discuss the topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, then at this time I would tender 1D7030, 1D7031, and 1D7032 for purposes of the photograph illustrations only.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that Mr. Ivetic then prepare the photographs. There is a lot of written text, including blog posts and advertisements on the -- on the document. I would object to him putting -- admitting it in its current form. We should --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Should we then mark it for identification, Mr. Ivetic, and that you prepare a cleaned copy --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, the numbers for these documents to be marked for identification are.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D7030 receives number D536. Document 1D7031 receives number D537. And document 1D7032 receives number D538, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They're all marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, and now I'd like to focus on the launcher that was used to launch aerial bombs by your brigade. Could you describe the rail or track on which the bomb was launched. Was there any mechanism to keep the bomb steady or straight?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that there were rails, what I meant was that this is something that makes it possible for the air bomb to get the right trajectory. As for the mode, the mechanisms that enabled this, I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How would the launch rail of this modified launcher compare to the launch tube of the M-63 Plamen which we saw in a picture, in terms of its length?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of Plamen it is shorter, and these rails through which the air bomb was launched are longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now today you were asked about the sound made by these rocket engines when they ignite. Do you know how long these rocket engines would burn and create sound upon being launched?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can call up again P6616.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I would like to focus for the moment on the items that are grey and cylindrical in nature that are in front of the truck, in front of the launcher. Could you identify for us what are those items?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could move to some follow-up questions about the air bomb launched at Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently you're interested to know what it is. Is there any way to agree with the Prosecution on it? Are these perhaps rockets that could be loaded into the launchers? I don't know but --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I could ask for a stipulation on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe they are rockets rather than launch tubes, but I don't know what Mr. Groome's position on that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then we have to be very clear. But I see 32 cylindrical features a bit higher up on what Mr. Groome referred to as the turret, right or wrong, and you were referring to the -- what we see --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In front of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- between that, in front of that, just behind the cabin of the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any understanding as to what that could be. Is that projectiles launched by this --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's certainly my understanding, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's the Defence understanding as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then -- so it's more or less ammunition for this launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The other day, at transcript page 23202, you stated that you received information from international observers and UNPROFOR and after you received information from your observers, and that you reported to General Milosevic where the bomb had fallen. What is it that you were told about where the bomb had fallen when you reported to General Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received my first information from my own observers who observed the flight of the air bomb and its dissent, and they said that it fell near the target. And the next information I received a few hours after it was launched from the members of the French battalion of UNPROFOR who said to me that a bomb had been launched from my positions, a bomb that fell close to the school, and that it hit a house. They said that there were guards in that house, and I think that they showed me an image showing the leg of a soldier in uniform. So that is the information -- the first information that I received about the landing of that air bomb. Also they said to me that they cannot give me anymore specific information because the commander of the 104th Brigade does not allow the military observers or the members of UNPROFOR to get even close to the place where the air bomb fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now today when you were dealing with the photograph P6618 of the school, you mentioned some photos shown to you by UNPROFOR. Are these the photos you're now talking about or are they some type of different photographs?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see any photographs here that I had seen at the UNPROFOR members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I seek clarification of one issue. You said UNPROFOR was not allowed to come any closer to the point of impact. Nevertheless, they told you that there were guards in that house and that you think they showed you an image showing the leg of a soldier in uniform. How can you produce such a photograph if you're not allowed anywhere close to the point of impact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not familiar with the details. I don't know, believe me. I just know that I was told that even the military observers, or they, were not allowed to get close to the spot where the bomb had impacted. They could not carry out an on-site investigation even.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you told us that you were shown a photograph which would give those details, not just a leg but even a leg in uniform. If -- and, at the same time, you told us that they were not even allowed to get even close to the place where the air bomb fell. I'm asking about your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know where they got that photograph and who they got it from, whether it was taken by some official of theirs or somebody else. But I know for sure that I did, indeed, see that photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did you see that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think a few hours after the explosion they showed me this photograph. I don't know what this camera is called now. You take a picture and the picture is there straight away. So that's the kind of picture that they took and that's what they showed me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have a follow-up question to this topic. You said: "They showed me the photograph." Who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Members of the French battalion of UNPROFOR who went to the scene to see where the bomb had fallen and in order to carry out an on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You said members of the French battalion. How many were there when you had this discussion with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as far as I can remember, there was one leader of a patrol, and there were or two or three other men with him: An officer, a captain, and two men escorting him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who was talking to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The captain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What did he say exactly with respect to the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He came to see me to inform me that he had received information that from our positions an air bomb had been launched, and he came to find out whether that was correct, whether it came from our positions. When I confirmed that to him, then I asked him," were you there?" And he said, "Yes." And he showed me this photograph, and he said," here it is, where it fell, and how it fell." And that's what we talked about. Nothing more than that. Nothing in great detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did he hand over the photograph to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he did not. I'm didn't ask for it and he didn't want to hand it over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How do you know that he didn't want to hand it over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, from experience, I know that it is their document. They don't give it to us. They just let us see it and then they keep it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That means that he did not hand it over but you don't know if he didn't want to hand it over; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. I assume that he did not want to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one more question in this respect. When Judge Fluegge asked you about who "they" were, you said: "Members of the French battalion of UNPROFOR who went to the scene to see where the bomb had fallen in order to carry out an on-site investigation." Now less than a page before this, you said: "They could not carry out an on-site investigation even." So one moment you tell us that they could not carry out an on-site investigation, and one page later you tell us that they showed you a photograph and "they" were those who went to the scene to see where the bomb had fallen and in order to carry out an on-site investigation. Have you any explanation for this apparent inconsistency? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. Probably I didn't explain it properly. They went to the scene and they wanted to carry out an on-site investigation; that is to say, they got close to the place where the air bomb had fallen and they wanted to carry out an on-site investigation. At that moment, the commander of the 104th Brigade came up and he prohibited them from approaching the scene. They had to leave and he no longer allowed them access to that place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Earlier you said that they were not -- they would not allow the military observers or the members of the UNPROFOR to get even close to the place, and now you say they went closely there, then they moved away again, and then later on they were not given access to the scene any further. Is that how we have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, probably I did not speak with full precision. The last thing I said is fully accurate information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And now again the photograph. Did they explain where this leg was found by them and photographed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they said that the bomb fell and destroyed a house and they managed to take this photograph. What was clearly depicted in that photograph was the leg of a soldier from the knee downwards in uniform. I don't know. It was a long time ago. I cannot recall all the details involved but that is the way it was, basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Where did they tell you where they found this leg? Inside the house, outside the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The house had been destroyed and it's on the rubble, on this pile of bricks. That's where this leg was protruding. That's the way it was, roughly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was exactly there where the house was destroyed. What does that tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can call up P6618, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we wait for it, sir, I can identify it as a picture that Mr. Groome showed you today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to turn to page 3 of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now the building that has an A-S and an arrow pointing to it, I'd like to direct your attention to a structure or building that appears to be of a grey colour that is perpendicular to that building marked A-S and that goes toward the location that is marked G10. Are you able to identify what is that building, perpendicular to the building marked A-S and going toward the location marked G10?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now for artillery or mortars, how close is a shell required to land to the intended target in order to be qualified as a successful fire mission under both categories of fire missions that you identified earlier?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Objection, compound question. It deals with both artillery and mortars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could you please split up --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you also give a kind of framework in which you should judge whether it was successful or not. I mean, sometimes I hear people considering matters being very successful where I would have some doubt, but then the problem is that there is no clear framework for judging that. So could you please make that part of your examination as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First of all, sir, you have told us that you are not an artilleryman. Do you feel that you are able to tell us about, let's say first, mortars? What is the beaten zone of a mortar launcher?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the calibre of mortar. It is considered that the target had been hit if it falls within the zone of a diameter of a successful mission for that projectile. If it's 82 millimetres, for instance, if I remember correctly, it's about 30 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And do you feel comfortable to answer a similar question in relation to artillery rounds and their beaten zone?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. With artillery pieces, since they are of larger calibre, the diameter of a beaten zone is larger. It ranges from 70 to 80 metres, depending on the type of asset. And if it's a Howitzer, it depends on the type of Howitzer, if it's a compact fuse or some other type of shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, neither the cross-examination nor the direct examination dealt with this concept of beaten zone. Could we establish that the witness knows what this means and, maybe for my own edification, understand what he understands that term to be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you're invited to follow up the suggestion made by Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, in your answers you've talked about a zone of a diameter, and you've identified that diameter for purposes of both an 82-millimetre mortar and an artillery. Can you explain for us what you mean by "this zone"? What is this zone called in the military parlance of the former Yugoslav armed forces?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the radius of lethal zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And is it -- what is your understanding of a beaten zone, which was the terminology that I used? If you have one. You may not.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You nevertheless answered it, Witness. Or do you mean the previous question or the question now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not understand the last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what was your understanding of a beaten zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My understanding of the concept of radius of lethal zone? If a shell hits a target, if the target is within the area of the radius of lethal zone, it is considered as a successful hit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the question was what do you understand by beaten zone, or are you unfamiliar with that expression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you answered a question which used that expression. Could I, before we take a break, invite the parties to make a clear distinction between the effect of an exploding shell and the precision in firing such a shell, because these are two different matters. The effect of a shell, depending perhaps on fuse used or surroundings, may -- is expected to be the same because it depends on the characterisation of the shell itself; whereas, the precision of firing a shell and hitting a target or landing where it was intended to land is a different matter and has more to do with the technology of firing than with the characteristics of the shell itself. And I got the feeling that the two are perhaps a bit confused in the last few questions. We take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, apart from number of questions, any idea on how much time they would take if not interrupted by the Judges?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think 35 to 40 minutes should suffice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the witness was thoroughly cross-examined and therefore the Chamber allows you to use such time. We take a break and will resume at half past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be brought in, Mr. Ivetic, I don't know whether it will ever come to tendering the complete video, perhaps depending on your conversations with Mr. Groome. But for a video to be tendered and therefore potentially be admitted into evidence, the Registry would need three copies of the video on a CD with a 65 ter number indicated on the CD: One for the OTP, one for the Chamber, and one for the Registry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and a related surrogate sheet and, if need be, transcripts uploaded in e-court under the same 65 ter number. That's what it would require to have it in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my understanding as well, Your Honours. That's why I did not seek to tender it to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yup.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One other matter I could direct Your Honours' attentions to, the questions before the break about the -- about the leg. I can direct Your Honours to another witness who testified about this, an eye-witness, 9173, lines 18 through 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for assisting us, Mr. Ivetic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could please revisit P592. And this will be the order of General Milosevic which was discussed in cross-examination relating to the Hrasnica incident. Now, first of all, sir, General go not identify a specific target for you. What maps did General Milosevic have at the corps level as opposed to the maps at the brigade level in relation to targets?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have the scale in mind, the difference was that at corps level, the scale was 1:100.000. At the brigade level, the scale was 1:50.000 and 1:25.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My question was a little bit more specific. Did General Milosevic have access to your map identifying brigade targets?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did have knowledge of the basic targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now returning to this order on our screens, the area that is mentioned where the ABiH is attacking in the first paragraph, are you familiar with the terrain and the positioning of the forces so as to tell us what would have happened if the ABiH further advanced in this area?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, the ABiH carried out an attack on the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade. There was a danger of its position being taken, which would mean that they would be able to enter Vojkovic. In that settlement, there were several thousand Serb inhabitants, some local and some refugees. The consequences would have been disastrous for the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now this order mentions in the second paragraph: "In order to thwart the enemy and give them a warning so that they are forced to accept this truce ..." Do you know what truce General Milosevic is talking about in this order?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since there was combat, obviously there was no truce to speak of. However, to force them into asking for a truce, General Milosevic issued this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now we also watched a video from Martin Bell during cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- dated 7 April, 1995. And the voice-over on that video starts: "The cease-fire appears to go crumbling rapidly." Do you recall if the Muslim offensive and, indeed, the Hrasnica aerial bomb firing occurred during the period of time of a cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The answer has been given, but I just wonder about the appropriateness of asking such a question when the witness has said just a few lines before "obviously there was no truce to speak of."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I believe we are allowed to refresh the recollection of a witness. And surely by a video that the Prosecution tendered, I think that is an appropriate question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no need for a ruling. Mr. Groome asked himself whether it was appropriate, yes or not. Apparently there is some difference of view. The question has been answered. We'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, at transcript page 23224, you stated that a commander is duty-bound according to international law of war to evacuate civilian population to avoid civilian casualties. And this was in relation to Fikret Prevljak. In your opinion, what Prevljak did during this time-period in Hrasnica, was it in compliance with that duty?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think he did that. His population -- or the population on his side did not even go to shelters. They freely moved about. I don't know whether it was on his orders or whether they disobeyed any of his orders is something I cannot discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you did as a commander when picking locations for your own military headquarters so as to comply with this duty?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My command post was situated at the beginning of a large avenue outside the urban part of Ilidza towards the source of the Bosna River. It is several hundred metres away from the nearest houses. In doing so, we made sure that any enemy artillery fire or mortar fire aimed at our command would be received by us, rather than having civilians as collateral damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And where was this location in reference to the front line with the ABiH? How close was it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The nearest position was near the forestry school and the institute, so several hundred metres away. I would say between 250 and 300 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did your headquarters encounter incoming fire from the ABiH; and, if so, how frequently?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly we did. The trees around the headquarters were torn apart and branches broken. They mostly received artillery fire. We also had two people killed, or perhaps three. They were guards securing the command post who were killed by their artillery from Hrasnica, Igman, and Sokolovic Kolonija.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to move to another topic. Today at temporary transcript page 20, line 1, you started talking about the investigation into the first Markale incident and you were interrupted by Mr. Groome. I'd ask you to complete your answer as to what happened after you were named a member of a commission to investigate the first Markale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question that I asked the witness was whether he had any paperwork. I did not ask him to go into any kind of detailed explanation, so I'd suggest that any re-examination should be limited to my query, which was simply whether there was the paperwork.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, it's really my recollection that Mr. Groome was primarily interested in any documentation and that in relation to his previous question about how written documents would support whether there was any investigation ordered or ... Would you please stick to that rather than to revisit the whole of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Markale.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I could perhaps then come to a more pointed question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, was the commission that you were part of permitted to perform an investigation as to the Markale shelling, the first Markale shelling?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Our UNPROFOR liaison officer provided information to the extent that the Muslim side disagreed with our being part of an expert team that was to analyse what had actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And was there anything for you to report as a result?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we didn't even go --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I renew my objection. This was all in reference to paragraph 108 where the witness says this bit about the commission. He wasn't challenged on that in any way. The second part of the paragraph says: "General Milosevic called me and ordered me to establish the facts." It was whether there was any paperwork with respect to General Milosevic asking him to establish the facts. That's what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's how I understood it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, my question was based upon your guidance at temporary transcript page 62, lines 5 through -- pardon me, 9 through 13, where you said: "Mr. Groome was primarily interested in any documentation and that in relation to his previous question about how written documents that would support whether there was any investigation ordered." I think this information does go to that question that Your Honour raised and introduced into the record of whether there was any evidence of it being ordered, and this explains why there isn't any documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me read the question again. I think even the question as rephrased did not follow my guidance. It's about ordering to investigate rather than how another party may have permitted. It was about the ordering. It was about the internal communication within the VRS, rather than what happened after that. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, I'd like to talk about the attack or the firing upon a UN convoy on the Igman mountain road that Mr. Groome asked you about at transcript page 23246. First of all, can you tell us if you had any understanding or agreement with UNPROFOR about the use of that road.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The official route for UNPROFOR movement was the highway between Sarajevo, Ilidza, Blazuj, and Kobiljaca and onto Kiseljak. And for the most part during the war, that was the route used. However, in the last year of the war, for reasons unbeknownst to me, they started using the road via Igman. It is a forest, unpaved road which had been cut through the woods in order to pull out tree trunks from Igman that had been done before the war. Until then, the road had been used by the ABiH alone. But at some point in the war, UNPROFOR began using it. We frequently discussed that topic, and they told me that they only relied on the road not to escort anything but simply for their personnel to return from touring positions on Mount Igman. However, in this specific case, the road was also used at the time UNPROFOR soldiers were pulling back to their base at around 6.00 p.m. At 6.00 p.m., all UNPROFOR members withdrew from all roads and positions to their base. I also tried to explain that it starts to get dark at the time, and there is a large spring of water there causing much fog in the area often; thus, limiting visibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what was the specific agreement you had with UNPROFOR as to the use of that mountain Igman road?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a specific agreement that the road would not be used for humanitarian convoy movements because there was no need to do so. There was a route agreed upon by the Main Staff which was supposed to be used. Even if they did the Igman -- use the Igman road, it was to be used during the day-time, and that is why this happened. That road is partly shaded, and it started getting dark, and taking into account everything about what the Prosecutor said about the time of day, this could only be applied to a clear area. But, in this case, it is a forested area frequently covered in fog, and visibility is truly limited. For that reason, I agreed with UNPROFOR not to use the road to escort any convoys but that convoys should use the route I described a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Prior to this incident where the convoy was fired upon, did UNPROFOR use the road during daylight hours?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. UNPROFOR used the route, as I said, in order to move their combat vehicles which were visibly marked and painted white. They used it to move between Hrasnica, Igman, and further in the field towards Bjelasnica where they toured ABiH positions and the lines of separation, but they exclusively did so during daylight hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: On those occasions when they used the road during daylight hours, did your forces engage and fire upon UNPROFOR on that road?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now after this shooting occurred, first of all, when is the next time you had direct contact with an UNPROFOR officer?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day. The French UNPROFOR commander came to see me. It was his custom to stay in touch with me frequently. I understood his visit as his wish to find out what had actually happened on the Igman road, but I did not tackle the topic first, and he didn't put any questions in that regard. It was my impression that it was his tacit understanding as to why we engaged him on that road. That was my understanding. He didn't even refer to it, but I understood it to mean that he was aware of the agreement that the road should not be used for movement of humanitarian convoys for reasons of abusing it to that end.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, did either this UNPROFOR officer from, I believe, the French -- you say the French commander or any other UNPROFOR officer ever lodge a complaint with you in relation to this incident of the firing upon UNPROFOR vehicles on the Mount Igman road?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. There were no protests coming from their side because there was no engagement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now this meeting with the UNPROFOR French commander that occurred the day after the incident, how would you describe the tone of that meeting and the demeanour of the French general -- pardon me, French commander?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a routine meeting. We discussed the existing problems and how best to deal with them. As I said, at no point in time did he refer to the incident on the Igman road. I understood it to mean that he saw it as a misunderstanding and that they actually moved during the time of day when -- which did not include the agreement. And the responsibility was brought to bear on UNPROFOR for escorting the humanitarian convoy at the specified time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I want to clarify with you something that you raised in response to a question from Mr. Groome. Did your forces fire a warning shot at the convoy on the Igman road that evening?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although we could have hit the convoy with the very first shell, because we had the route plotted, we fired the first round over their heads. Since they continued movement without ever stopping, we used the second round to hit a vehicle and it was then that the convoy stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How many total projectiles did your forces fire, including the shot over their heads?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One. Actually, one plus one, meaning two.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now the other day at transcript page 23250, you were describing this section of the road where you could target the vehicles and you said it was a couple of hundred metres with a mask and trees. Could you explain what you meant by this description?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could follow the convoy visually, especially during the night because of the flashes it created. We could follow it from the general area of Igman. However, the area of engagement of our cannon, T-12, which had been posted there exclusively for that person [as interpreted], they passed over only the lower part of the route we saw on the photograph shown by the Prosecutor. That is exactly the stretch I refer to. It is forested. And there is only one part of the road that is visible and only there can you engage anyone. I think the stretch is no longer than -- not longer than 2- or 300 metres. Had they gone through that stretch, they would have become unavailable. They would have been masked by trees. That is why they tried to cover that stretch as quickly as possible in order to avoid being hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now you say: "Had they gone through that stretch, they would have become unavailable." Unavailable for what?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could no longer control their movement. What is important at this moment is to know that we didn't know who it was. We didn't know if it was UNPROFOR or the ABiH. Because on the infrared device, due to the quality of the image, one cannot tell if it's an UNPROFOR or an ABiH vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If they had passed that 2- to 300 metre stretch, did you have other heavy weapons more inward in your lines that could reach and prevent those vehicles from coming closer to you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there would have been no other possibility to target them. We could engage them risking to hit another target which we did not intend to do so. I now only have in mind my brigade, whereas some other brigades may have had the opportunity to engage them along other stretches, but this was the only stretch where my unit could.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, I thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that exhausts the questions that I had for redirect examination, and I thank you for the time given for the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Judge Fluegge would have a question before we give an opportunity to the Prosecution to put further questions. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to clarify one matter and take you back to one portion of your testimony of today just to better understand. This is in relation to page 45, lines 13 to 17. Mr. Ivetic asked you: "What is your recollection of the type of rocket engines that were used for the three aerial bombs launched by your brigade?" Your answer was: "I think that Plamen rocket systems were used." Last week you were also asked about the Plamen system, and you said -- and this can be found on page 23162, line 10. You were asked about the Plamen rocket system, and then your answer was, I quote: "Not a single brigade of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps had a Plamen multi-rocket launcher." "Q. Did you have any rocket launcher system?" Your answer was: "My brigade didn't. And I say that categorically. The Plamen rocket system, according to the establishment of the JNA, could only be found in operative units of the corps and in the land forces, not as part of the equipment of tactical units." A little bit later on page 23180, you added to that the following. I quote: "When I stated that my brigade did not have this, I know that with 100 per cent certainty. The adjacent brigades they didn't either, according to establishment. Quite simply, a Plamen is not supposed to be in brigades, according to establishment." Can you help me to understand your testimony in that respect, especially in relation to the use of any Plamen equipment for the three aerial bombs?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by what I said, that my brigade didn't have multi-barrel rocket launchers, Plamen or any other weapons that could fire the Plamen rockets, other than air bombs. My logistics commander, or logistics assistant, obtained the required quantity of rockets from the logistical corps command only for air bombs, not for any other weapons that would use this Plamen ammunition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What I understood from your answer is that you didn't have any Plamen system in your brigade or in the adjacent brigades but your people were able to receive some parts of the system for use for the firing of the aerial bombs.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. As I said, we would receive the necessary elements to build the air bomb through our logistics organ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which parts of the Plamen system were used for the aerial bombs?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The engine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you explain that further? I don't fully understand what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was used were the projectiles of Plamen without the warhead, just the body of it with gunpowder charges that would enable the projectile to fly. They were used without the warheads. Only the body of the Plamen rockets was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have a few more questions for you as well about what the chronology on what happened during the day of the modified aerial bomb being fired at a target in Hrasnica. What time was it that the aerial bomb was fired?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, it was fired in the morning. I don't know exactly what time it was, though. I think it was in the early part of the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At what time did you get in touch with, as you said, the French -- the UNPROFOR French unit which reported to you about and gave that photograph? At what time was that, approximately?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was a few hours after the launching. I cannot remember all the details. This was 19 years ago, after all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where did you meet with them? Did they come to you, did you come to them?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came to my command. And the main reason that they came was to inform me that a bomb was launched from my positions, and they wanted information. So the goal of the visit was to establish whether it was launched from my brigade's AOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they tell you anything about what had happened to them when they went to the site of impact?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated a few times in my testimony that I'm not able to quote what they said, but the sense of it was that it was reported by their observers that an aerial bomb fell in Hrasnica and that they immediately sent out a patrol. When the patrol arrived on the scene, they wanted to conduct an investigation. They told me that military observers were present as well; I don't know from which country. But then they said that Fikret Prevljak came, the commander of the 104th Brigade, and told them to leave the area where the aerial bomb fell, and he did not allow them access there for the rest of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when was it then that they had taken those paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably before the commander arrived. They came, they were standing around, and then somebody reported to the commander that they had arrived and then he intervened. But I assume that they made the photographs while they were in Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber heard evidence that the French came after the UNMOs had been more or less restricted in their freedom of movement; apparently the site of impact being under control of the opposite armed forces. Do you have any explanation as to where the UNMOs were kept out and even lost their freedom of movement, why UNPROFOR would then have come and be free to photograph, take photographs, before, as you said, they were told to leave?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume what happened. The UNMOs had less authority than the UNPROFOR. There were more members of UNPROFOR and they were more robustly equipped, and you tried to avoid conflict with them as much as possible. UNMOs, however, were something else. And this is the only way that I can explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you any explanation as why these photographs that were shown to you never appeared anywhere in any document?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have an explanation. I might have some thoughts about it. When I suspected that there was a tunnel underneath the airport, I tried through my channels to find out some details. I was given a diagram by an UNPROFOR member, with the title: "Entre the tunnel," and that was where I suspected it was. Later, in a conversation with their commander, I tried to find out whether this tunnel existed or not, and he said, "No, no, this is just talk. It's unconfirmed information." It was a matter of them trying to co-operate with one or the other side. In this case, this was about people that I was frequently in contact with, and they showed me as a gesture of good will what it was that hit that particular area. That would be that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I have some difficulties in understanding exactly what you're telling us. Are you saying that UNPROFOR was friendly with you and for that reason they have shown the photograph to you but not to anyone else?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I meant. I understood it as a gesture of good will that they showed it to me. They didn't want to give it to me. I was shown the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that. But if you take a photograph of a scene immediately after an impact of a modified aerial bomb, showing to you is one. My question was about why that photograph never appeared anywhere in any report or that it was shared with the UNMOs or -- but it -- you seem to be the only one who have seen it apart from the person who showed it to you.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my testimony in the Karadzic case, I had the opportunity to see this photograph among the documents that were presented to me at the time. If you look carefully probably you can find this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if it was shown to you in the Karadzic case, I would expect the parties to -- to produce that, but -- any party -- this Chamber has no access to the evidence in the Karadzic case, so -- Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could we enquire who showed it to him? Who was the person that showed it to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us who showed it to you in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that during the preparation phase, one of the attorneys who was proofing me here in The Hague showed it to me. When I was talking on that topic, he showed me that photograph. Yes, yes, and that's when I saw it. I think that the lawyer in question was a Mr. Sladojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that makes the puzzle even greater. Because it might have been clearly in the interest of the Defence of Mr. Karadzic to bring that photograph to court and to confront you with that photograph. But that did not happen, if I understand you well? I think Mr. Mladic wants to consult with, again, admitted, even if at an inaudible volume. Could you ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said what I had said. I remember the photograph well. I think that I saw it here. As for how you can get it now, I don't know, but I can guarantee that you have the photograph, and I'm surprised that you haven't seen it yet. That's why I was talking about these details because I thought you -- you had seen it yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was the report about one leg coming out of the rubble?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber received evidence that to the extent there were any body parts, that it was two legs rather than one, and that did not originate from members of the French unit of UNPROFOR. Do you have any explanation for this -- oh, apparently there is some interpretation problem. Has it been resolved now? Yes. Okay. Then I restart. This Chamber received evidence that to the extent there were any body parts, that it was two legs rather than one, and that information did not originate from members of the French unit of UNPROFOR. Do you have any explanation as for the two legs against one and for another source than the French UNPROFOR members?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no comment. It's possible that you could see the other leg really well, but I noticed really well one leg up to the knee with camouflage uniform and a boot on the foot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they came to see you in your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To the extent you know, did they immediately go from the site of the impact to your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't really say. On the way from Hrasnica to me, they passed through the airport. Their base was at the airport. I don't know if in the meantime they stopped off at the battalion regiment command and then went on to visit me. I don't know that. But any road would lead them through their command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I also have one or two questions on a totally different topic, but Judge Fluegge would like to ask a follow-up question on the matter we just tackled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just to be very clear about that, you said you saw the photo which was shown to you during proofing for your testimony in the Karadzic case. Shown to you by a lawyer. And you thought it was Mr. Sladojevic. Can I take from your answer it was not used during your testimony in court?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not used, that's right. Nobody put any questions to me on that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have a question on a total different subject. You were asked about not destroying a target but nevertheless having been successful in engaging that target. Now, if you would target the headquarters or from -- at whatever level, company headquarters, battalion headquarters, would you -- would the aim be to paralyse them or to destroy them or ...

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably neutralise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when do you consider such a headquarter to be neutralised? Let's just assume that somewhere in a basement of a building there is a suspicion that there is headquarters of a company or whatever. When would you consider it to be neutralised?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it's destroyed, it means that the target cannot be used. If it's neutralised, then it can be used again after a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if, for example, let's just take the same example. Now a mortar shell falls at a distance of 100 and 150 metres from the building in which basement that headquarters was suspected to be present. Would that neutralise it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't strike that target with a mortar shell because that's something that's used for destroying a target out in the open. I would use, rather, a gun or a more precise weapon with a contact fuse which would then go through and neutralise the target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now let's stay away from whether the mortar would be the best one or you would rather find another type of shell. But if it would land at a distance of 100 metres from that headquarters, would the headquarters then be neutralised or would they not be neutralised?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The target was not neutralised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if a shell would fall at a claimed entrance of a headquarter, company headquarter, whatever headquarter, and it would miss by 100 to 150 metres, you would need to follow up because the target was neither neutralised nor destroyed. Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, just a few Your Honour, thank you. Further cross-examination by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I just want to return to this photograph again that you say you were shown by Mr. Sladojevic in your preparations for your Karadzic testimony. The first question that I have for you is: Is it your evidence that the picture that Mr. Sladojevic showed you was the same picture that was shown to you by the French UNPROFOR person?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that with any disagree of decisiveness. I don't know if the picture is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did the -- are you able to say with any degree of certainty whether the subject matter was the same; that is, maybe a photograph taken of the same scene but from a different angle and perhaps by a different person? Are you able to say that the subject matter was the same?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was it a Polaroid photo, what Mr. Sladojevic showed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not sure, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, through e-mail, I've just checked with my colleagues in the Karadzic team, and no such photo has ever been tendered in that case, so my question to you is: Did Mr. Sladojevic inform you that a decision had been taken to not use this photo which on its face appears to be rather important evidence?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not tell me that it would not be used. When we spoke about the point of impact and the damage it caused, I think that was when they showed me the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to go -- or return to the topic of the attack that you ordered on the convoy on Mount Igman on the 14th of July, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that 65 ter 10638 be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we're doing this, you gave some detailed evidence about conversations you had with a French commander, a French UNPROFOR commander. Can you tell us his name?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not difficult to check. I cannot remember his name, but you can find out who it was there in that period, what the name of the person was. I think they changed. Every 12 months or so there would be a new officer, so I don't remember that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The way you described your interaction with this officer, I had the impression that you had a good working relationship. You seemed to know each other quite well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All members of French UNPROFOR were officers I had daily communication with. They came to my location every day. It was nothing unusual. The same officers, when they went to the other side, probably had relations that were just as good. So it was not a question of friendship or anything. We're just talking about the usual good professional relationships, and we would be in contact any time that there would be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the person's first name or any part of their last name?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is probably more of a question for my UNPROFOR liaison officer, and I could give you his name if you would like, and then you can find out more details about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, it's your evidence that he showed you the photograph, so I'm interested in what you remember about the person. Do you remember what he looked like?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they always had helmets. I don't remember any details now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. The document I want is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you said in your evidence just a few minutes ago in response to Mr. Ivetic that during the last year of the war the UNPROFOR started to use the Igman road, and you said: "However, in the last year of the war, for reasons unbeknownst to me, they started using the road via Igman." Now this is a report, UNPROFOR weekly situation report, from the 8th of July, 1995. And I want to just focus on the highlights. If you look at the first page, we read: "Denied any freedom of movement by the Serbs" --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we need to go to the second page of the B/C/S and I'll start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "Denied any freedom of movement by the Serbs. UNPROFOR and UNHCR continue to use the Igman road." And then skipping to the next highlight, we read: "The humanitarian situation remains poor. The air-lift remains suspended as it has been for three months. The food warehouses are mostly empty. There is almost no water or electricity and no gas at all." Colonel Radojcic, I put it to you that you do know why they used the Igman road, and that's because you and other VRS officers in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps ensured that UNPROFOR and UNHCR could not bring any kind of humanitarian assistance into the city of Sarajevo by any road or by the airport. Isn't that the reason why they resorted to this dirt road through the woods up on Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question of movement of humanitarian aid convoys went considerably beyond the authority I had. I only acted on orders in this case. So if there was a problem, it was resolved at a level that was much higher than my own. In this case, to accuse me of having prevented people of obtaining humanitarian aid, that is incorrect, because I did not have such powers. It was for me only to carry out the orders I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 10638.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 10638 receives number P6620, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: 10. It shouldn't be -- it should be 6610 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's P6620.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Finally, sir, you also said in response to questions of Mr. Ivetic today that there was an agreement that the UNPROFOR would only use the Igman road in daylight hours. In fact, at T-65 you said: "They used it to move between Hrasnica, Igman, and further in the field towards Bjelasnica where they toured ABiH positions and the lines of separation, but they exclusively did so during daylight hours." Now, sir, P6619 is in evidence, and we know that sunset was at 8.27 p.m. Can you accept that an UNPROFOR convoy that's up on that hill at 6.30 to 6.50 that day, honestly believed that they were using that road per the agreement in the daylight hours? Can you accept that that's how they -- that they, in their view, they were abiding by any agreement to use that road in daylight hours?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, this agreement meant that vehicles of UNPROFOR could move around, not humanitarian aid convoys. Because at the level of the Main Staff, a route had been agreed upon along which the convoy would move. In this case, it wasn't the Igman route.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to the issue of timing, can you accept that UNPROFOR on the mountain at 6.30 to 6.50 in the evening honestly believed that with sunset an hour and a half to two hours away that they were travelling in daylight hours? Can you accept that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can ask you to speak to the UNPROFOR command, to ask them why their working hours were over at 1800 hours. I'm not in a position to say why they did it that way. They withdrew into their bases at 1800 hours precisely because it became dark and in order to avoid incidents. It was a war zone. We were only a couple of hundred metres away from the enemy, and it's very hard to say anything from this distance now. But in that actual situation, it is very hard to establish who was where at a given location.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But it's not hard to establish that at 6.30 to 6.50 it was daylight?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not daylight. I keep telling you that. That was the time I know -- I know what you're going to show me now and that is correct. It is correct the sunset comes later. But do go to Sarajevo and ask people there at 7.00 on the slopes of Mount Igman whether visibility is such at 7.00 p.m. that you can see whether that's an UNPROFOR vehicle or a BH army vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no other questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Weren't you offered to go together with the Office of the Prosecution to that place? You said -- because you said "but do go to Sarajevo and ask people there." You were invited to join any mission which, on the 14th of July, would see exactly how much light there would be, and I think you said you were not inclined to do that, isn't it? So the phrase: "Do go to Sarajevo," in view of your response earlier, any comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My reason for not going to Sarajevo is purely personal, and I wouldn't like to comment on that. It is nothing else but a personal reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I nevertheless would like you to tell us why, what that personal reason is. If you want to move into private session, fine as far as I'm concerned if you don't want the outside world. But the Chamber, since you're invoking those reasons, would like to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would ask if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am talking to you, you are talking to the Chamber. There is no reason to seek any contact with the Defence at this moment, eye contact. So if you want to go into private session, we'll do it. Otherwise, please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, ultimately I am going to tell you why I don't want to go to Sarajevo. Actually, the Muslims filed several criminal reports against me, and I'm afraid that my security would be jeopardized if I were to find myself in that area. That is the only reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if for good reasons you would be immune for arrest, would you go then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know why my presence there would be indispensable when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a different question. You said the reason why you wouldn't go there is you fear for being arrested. If I said if that fear for arrest would be removed, would you go there? Are you willing to go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have to think about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions triggered by the Bench. Then this concludes your testimony, Mr. Radojcic. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties. You had to stay for quite a while in The Hague. Now you can return. I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to put the following on the record. To the extent there may be any confusion on the transcript, which is only a temporary one, document 10638 has received number P6620 and not P6610. We take a break. And the parties -- well, of course, we still have to deal with the -- with the associated exhibits. I don't know where we are in preparations for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I thought Your Honours had said we would do that written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So I would propose that we do it in writing since there are quite a number of them, and it would be perhaps easiest for me to prepare a written submission and for the Prosecution to respond to the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had prepared a copy of the Defence exhibit list with the Prosecution's position. I can hold it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- or I can distribute it. So whatever suits the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be a good idea that you present it to Mr. Ivetic, that Mr. Ivetic considers your response when he considers whether or not to shorten his list of associated exhibits. And already also consider the reasons why you may oppose or not oppose in his further written submissions --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- still to be prepared. Then we'll wait for that. I think it's still worthwhile to start with the next witness after the break. We'll have a break of 20 minutes. We'll resume at 5 minutes past 2.00 and might forego the formalities with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom. I don't know who to address, but is it true that I see two documents on the list of associated exhibits with the same 65 ter number; that is, 1D02066?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. We noticed that mistake, and yesterday we provided a correction; 1D02066. That's the document. It has been corrected. It's now 1D02067.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. I missed the correction. But we should have looked at it. Good afternoon, Mr. Tusevljak. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Tusevljak. Mr. Tusevljak, there are only a few minutes further to go today but we'll make a start with your testimony. You'll be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic, you find him to your left, and Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Stojanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave just one more thing. Since we agreed with the Prosecution on how this statement will be dealt with, 65 ter 1D02065, I would like to ask my learned friend Mr. Shin to make you aware of the agreements that we have reached and also in terms of the obligations that we have vis-à-vis the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Your Honours. Mr. President, I discussed with Mr. Stojanovic the redaction of certain sentences in that statement because they relate to a Scheduled Incident which has been dropped from our indictment. So in the interests of a more stream-lined process, we'd admit that agreement. My understanding is that -- specifically it's in paragraph 25 of that statement, and it relates to Incident F10. My understanding is that my learned friend has not yet had a chance to prepare the redacted version but they will be able to do that before tendering the document tomorrow morning, but I'll leave that to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think this is accepted by the Chamber to leave out matters which are dropped from the indictment. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just another piece of information, something that we agreed upon. You know that we have that obligation to stipulate on that exchange of maps. Mr. Shin and I have been working on this, and I believe that we will provide you with more specific information very soon. And with your leave, I would now like to start examining this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, could you please speak slowly and state for the record your full name and surname.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Slobodan Tusevljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell the Trial Chamber whether at one point in time you gave a statement to General Mladic's Defence about various things that happened about which we had questioned you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D1627, could we please have that in e-court now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, we're just going to wait for a moment to have the English version up as well. Thank you. The information on this page, are these your details and is the signature on this page yours?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please take a look at the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, is this also your signature?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next thing I wish to ask you is as follows. For the purposes of Mr. Karadzic's defence, did you also provide a more extensive statement about the same things that we from the Defence of General Mladic discussed with you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D02065 in e-court, the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the signature on this last page of the statement that you gave in Mr. Karadzic's case, is this also your signature?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the preparations carried out for your appearance in court today --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, Your Honours, could we please go back to 1D1627? 1D1627. Could we please have the second page on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you draw my attention to something that you noticed together with me that in paragraph 2 there is a typographical error. When you speak about snipers, it actually pertains to paragraph 26 of the statement that you gave in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 3 of this statement, did you also indicate to us that there is a typographical error, and you say here: "I discuss in paragraphs 2 and 3 of the statement," et cetera, it should be paragraph 26 in relation to snipers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you also indicate to us that in paragraph 4 this sentence, which reads as follows: "It was not possible to hit a tram from the Metalka building." And this has nothing to do with what you were asked about and you did not notice this when you were signing the statement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I noticed it only later and then I said to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That we should delete that from the statement.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, it has nothing to do with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And also in paragraph 7, you explain to us that the attack of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina against your positions was on the 11th of June and the second one was on the 12th of June. And then the front line was not moved.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There has just been this inversion of dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, one clarification in relation to paragraph 4. Are you suggesting to delete the entire paragraph 4 or only the sentence, or the part of the sentence, "it was not possible to hit a tram from the Metalka building." What is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. As I said to the OTP as well, that is what the witness cautioned us about, the sentence that reads as follows:"... it was not possible to hit a tram from the Metalka building." That sentence should be deleted from paragraph 4 and the rest remains unchanged. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, this is what I'm asking you. This statement, now that these corrections have been made, as for the typographical errors, and also this phrase in paragraph 4 should be deleted, and then in paragraph 7 you also made these corrections, given all of this, does this fully correspond to what you wish to say and what you did say and what your recollection is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D1627, Your Honours, could that please be admitted into evidence? Whereas 1D2065, should that be admitted into evidence only for identification. However, we've already agreed with the Prosecution, I think, that we would like to redact two sentences from paragraph 25, those that have to do with Incident F10 which is no longer in our indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, number -- 65 ter oh, no, the doc ID I -- 1D1627 receives number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number D539, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D539 is admitted into evidence. For 1D2065, we'd like to have a number reserved.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The reserved number would be D540, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That number is reserved for the newly to be uploaded version of the statement with a redaction in paragraph 25. We adjourn for the day. Mr. Stojanovic, it's time. Witness, before you leave this courtroom, I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony. Now, it's not that you've given that much testimony today, although content, yes, because at least one of your statements is now admitted into evidence. But also for any testimony still to be given tomorrow. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day and will resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 3rd of July, 9.30 in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 3rd day of July, 2014, at 9.30 a.m. 23 24 25
